questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is the water potential of pure water at 298 K and 101.3 kPa?
questions.hint: It is the reference value.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State a unit used for water potential.
questions.hint: It is a unit of pressure.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: In which direction does water move by osmosis?
options: From lower to higher water potential
From higher to lower water potential
Always from lower to higher pressure potential
questions.answer: From higher to lower water potential
questions.hint: Compare this to a gradient that runs downhill.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What effect does adding solutes have on the solute potential of water?
questions.hint: Solutes reduce the tendency of water to move.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State the term for a solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell.
questions.hint: The prefix means 'above'.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A plant cell has a solute potential of −800 kPa and a pressure potential of +300 kPa. Calculate its water potential in kPa.
questions.hint: Add the two components, keeping their signs.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A plant cell has a water potential of −450 kPa and a solute potential of −700 kPa. Calculate its pressure potential in kPa.
questions.hint: Rearrange the water potential equation.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A plant cell with a solute potential of −600 kPa is placed in pure water and reaches equilibrium. Calculate its pressure potential in kPa.
questions.hint: At equilibrium, the cell's water potential equals that of pure water.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Cell A has a water potential of −400 kPa and adjacent cell B has −700 kPa. What is the net movement of water?
options: Equal in both directions, with solutes moving to A
questions.hint: Identify the higher water potential. Remember that −400 is greater than −700.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A plant cell with a water potential of −300 kPa is placed in a solution of −500 kPa. What happens?
options: Water enters and pressure potential rises
Water leaves and pressure potential falls
There is no net movement of water
questions.answer: Water leaves and pressure potential falls
questions.hint: Compare the two values, then think about the wall.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What is the approximate pressure potential of a fully plasmolysed plant cell?
questions.hint: The membrane is no longer pressing against the wall.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Where in a plant is a negative pressure potential commonly found?
options: In the sap under tension in xylem
In the vacuole of a turgid root cell
questions.answer: In the sap under tension in xylem
questions.hint: Think about transpiration pull.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why does an animal cell in a hypotonic solution burst rather than reach a high pressure potential?
options: It has no cell wall to resist expansion
It has a very high solute potential
Its water potential is always zero
questions.answer: It has no cell wall to resist expansion
questions.hint: What in a plant cell allows pressure potential to build up?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Plant tissue has a mass of 12.5 g before and 11.0 g after being placed in a solution. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Use a minus sign for a loss.
questions.hint: Divide the change in mass by the initial mass.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A plant cell has been placed in a hypotonic solution. Explain, using solute potential and pressure potential, how its water potential changes as it takes in water.
questions.hint: Consider how each component changes as water enters.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Design an experiment to determine the water potential of potato tissue. Include the variables, how the results would be processed, and how the value would be obtained.
questions.hint: Think of a range of solutions with known water potentials, and the point of no mass change.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which statement defines osmosis?
options: Net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane to a higher solute concentration
Movement of solutes across a membrane to a lower solute concentration
Active movement of water using ATP
Movement of water through xylem to the leaves
questions.answer: Net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane to a higher solute concentration
questions.hint: Focus on what moves and through what.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State the term for a solution with a lower solute concentration than the cell's cytoplasm.
questions.hint: The prefix means 'below'.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State the term for a solution with the same solute concentration as the cell's cytoplasm.
questions.hint: The prefix means 'equal'.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What happens to an animal cell placed in distilled water?
options: It takes in water and may burst
questions.answer: It takes in water and may burst
questions.hint: The cytoplasm has more solutes than distilled water.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What happens to a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution?
options: The membrane pulls away from the cell wall
It gains water and becomes turgid
questions.answer: The membrane pulls away from the cell wall
questions.hint: Water leaves the cell.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State the name of the process in which a plant cell's membrane pulls away from its wall as water is lost.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the cytoplasm as it shrinks.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why does a plant cell not burst in a hypotonic solution?
options: Its cell wall resists further expansion
Its membrane is impermeable to water
It pumps all water out using ATP
questions.answer: Its cell wall resists further expansion
questions.hint: Which structure do plant cells have that animal cells lack?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State the term for the pressure of cell contents against a plant cell wall.
questions.hint: Think about a firm plant cell that is not wilting.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Why are organs for transplant kept in a cold isotonic solution?
options: To prevent net water gain or loss by the cells
To provide the cells with oxygen
To stop bacteria from reproducing by osmosis
To dissolve the blood in the vessels
questions.answer: To prevent net water gain or loss by the cells
questions.hint: Consider what hypotonic and hypertonic solutions would do to tissue.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A potato cylinder has a mass of 5.0 g before and 5.6 g after being placed in a sucrose solution. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
questions.hint: Divide the change in mass by the initial mass.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A potato cylinder has a mass of 8.0 g before and 6.8 g after being placed in a sucrose solution. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Use a minus sign for a loss.
questions.hint: Divide the change in mass by the initial mass.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: In an osmosis practical, why is percentage change in mass used rather than change in mass?
options: The cylinders may have different initial masses
It removes the need for a balance
Mass cannot be measured accurately in grams
It increases the rate of osmosis
questions.answer: The cylinders may have different initial masses
questions.hint: Think about making fair comparisons.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: In a practical testing tissue in a range of sucrose solutions, which is the independent variable?
questions.hint: It is the factor deliberately changed by the investigator.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A graph shows no change in mass of tissue at 0.3 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. What does this suggest?
options: The solution is isotonic with the tissue
questions.answer: The solution is isotonic with the tissue
questions.hint: What does no net water movement imply?

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Outline a method to estimate the solute concentration of potato tissue using a range of sucrose solutions. Include how you would control variables and process your results.
questions.hint: Think about the range of solutions, controlled variables, measurements and the graph.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Explain why intravenous fluids given to patients must be isotonic with blood plasma, referring to the effects of hypotonic and hypertonic solutions on red blood cells.
questions.hint: Consider both possible errors separately.

bus-hl.topic: Organizational structure — HL: project-based structures and Handy's shamrock

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: In Handy's shamrock organization, how many groups make up the workforce?
questions.hint: Consider the leaves of the plant.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: In Handy's shamrock, which group contains the essential permanent managers and specialists?
questions.hint: They are central to the organization's knowledge.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which group of Handy's shamrock is made up of part-time and temporary workers?
questions.hint: Their hours rise and fall with demand.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: In Handy's shamrock, what is the contractual fringe?
options: External specialists who provide outsourced services
questions.answer: External specialists who provide outsourced services
questions.hint: These people work for a fee, not a wage.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What characterizes a project-based organization?
options: Work is arranged around teams formed for specific projects
Each employee does the same task permanently
All decisions are taken by the founder
Departments are fixed by function forever
questions.answer: Work is arranged around teams formed for specific projects
questions.hint: Teams come together for a task and then disband.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A key benefit of a project-based structure for a consultancy is:
options: Specialists can be brought together flexibly for each client
Job roles never need to change
There is no need for managers to coordinate
questions.answer: Specialists can be brought together flexibly for each client
questions.hint: Think about how client needs differ.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A key drawback of project-based work for employees is:
options: Reduced job security when projects end
questions.answer: Reduced job security when projects end
questions.hint: Consider what happens after the final deadline.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: State the term for moving part of a firm's work to an external supplier, as used in Handy's contractual fringe.
questions.hint: The task moves outside the business.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A firm has 1 director, 5 managers each with a span of control of 7, and each manager's team is made up only of front-line staff. Calculate the total number of employees including the director and managers.
questions.hint: Find the front-line staff first.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which pair correctly matches a structure with a likely characteristic?
options: Flat structure: narrow spans of control
Matrix structure: one line manager only
questions.hint: Count how many people a message passes through.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Why might a business with an uncertain demand choose the shamrock model?
options: It can adjust labour costs quickly
It guarantees permanent jobs for all
It removes the need for a core team
questions.answer: It can adjust labour costs quickly
questions.hint: Think about which costs can rise or fall easily.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which term describes the extent to which a manager retains ultimate accountability after delegating a task?
questions.hint: It is the part of the job that is not passed on.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: State the name of the structure in which staff report to both a functional manager and a project manager.
questions.hint: Think of a grid.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Explain two reasons why core employees in a shamrock organization may be more motivated than those in the flexible labour force.
questions.hint: Compare job security, pay or involvement in decisions.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Analyse how a change from a tall hierarchy to a project-based organization could affect internal communication.
questions.hint: Consider both speed and possible confusion.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A film production company employs most of its crew only for the length of each film. Evaluate the use of a project-based, shamrock-type structure for this company.
questions.hint: Consider flexibility, costs, quality and morale, then reach a judgement.

bus-sl.topic: Organizational structure: hierarchy, span of control and delegation

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What does an organization chart show?
options: The formal structure of authority and reporting in a business
The market share of a business
The marketing plan of a business
questions.answer: The formal structure of authority and reporting in a business
questions.hint: Think about who reports to whom.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: State the term for the number of subordinates directly accountable to one manager.
questions.hint: It describes how wide a manager's direct responsibility stretches.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: State the term for the line through which authority passes from the top of a hierarchy to the bottom.
questions.hint: Orders travel along it.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of the following best defines delegation?
options: Passing authority for a task to a subordinate
Moving a business to another country
questions.answer: Passing authority for a task to a subordinate
questions.hint: A manager gives someone else the power to act.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which feature is typical of a tall organizational structure?
options: Many levels of hierarchy and narrow spans of control
Few levels of hierarchy and wide spans of control
Employees reporting to two bosses at once
questions.answer: Many levels of hierarchy and narrow spans of control
questions.hint: Picture the shape of the chart.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business has one managing director, 4 department managers, and 6 employees reporting to each department manager. Calculate the total number of people in the organization.
questions.hint: Add up all three levels.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A hospital ward manager has 3 senior nurses reporting directly to her, and each senior nurse supervises 8 nurses. State the span of control of the ward manager.
questions.hint: Count direct reports only.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What is meant by centralization?
options: Most decisions are taken by senior managers
Most decisions are taken by local branch staff
Most work is done by external contractors
questions.answer: Most decisions are taken by senior managers
questions.hint: Consider where decision-making power sits.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A likely effect of widening a manager's span of control is that:
options: Each subordinate receives less close supervision
The number of hierarchical levels must rise
questions.answer: Each subordinate receives less close supervision
questions.hint: The manager's time is shared among more people.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which change is called delayering?
options: Removing one or more levels of a hierarchy
Adding a new level of supervisors
questions.answer: Removing one or more levels of a hierarchy
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the height of the chart.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A matrix structure is best described as one in which:
options: Employees are organized by project teams as well as by function
Decisions are always taken by one owner
There is only one level of hierarchy
questions.answer: Employees are organized by project teams as well as by function
questions.hint: An engineer might also belong to a product team.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A possible disadvantage of a matrix structure is:
options: Employees may have conflicting instructions from two managers
Teams cannot be created for projects
questions.answer: Employees may have conflicting instructions from two managers
questions.hint: Think about who an employee answers to.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: State the term for the transfer of decision-making authority away from head office to lower levels of an organization.
questions.hint: It is the opposite of keeping decisions at the top.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Explain two advantages to a growing retailer of delegating decisions to its store managers.
questions.hint: Consider both the store managers and senior leaders.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Using the concept of span of control, explain why a flat structure may suit a small software company.
questions.hint: Think about communication and the type of employee.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A family-owned restaurant chain is opening 20 new branches. Discuss whether it should become more decentralized.
questions.hint: Weigh local knowledge against consistency of the brand.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: An element with the configuration [Ar] 4s² is found in:
questions.hint: The principal quantum number and the number of outer electrons give the position.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the atomic number of the element in period 3, group 13.
questions.hint: Count across from sodium.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which species has the smallest radius?
questions.hint: These ions are isoelectronic, so compare nuclear charges.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which correctly compares the radii of a chlorine atom and a chloride ion?
options: The Cl⁻ ion is larger than the Cl atom
The Cl atom is larger than the Cl⁻ ion
questions.answer: The Cl⁻ ion is larger than the Cl atom
questions.hint: Consider repulsion when an electron is added.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of aluminium lower than that of magnesium?
options: The outer electron of Al is in a higher-energy 3p sub-level
Al has a smaller nuclear charge than Mg
The outer electron of Al is in the 3s sub-level
Al has more electron shells than Mg
questions.answer: The outer electron of Al is in a higher-energy 3p sub-level
questions.hint: Compare the sub-levels from which the electrons are removed.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why is the first ionisation energy of sulfur lower than that of phosphorus?
options: Repulsion between paired electrons in a 3p orbital
Sulfur has a lower nuclear charge
Sulfur has a smaller shell of electrons
Phosphorus has its outer electrons in the 3d sub-level
questions.answer: Repulsion between paired electrons in a 3p orbital
questions.hint: Draw the 3p orbitals as boxes for each element.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the oxidation state of phosphorus in P₄O₁₀. Give your answer as a number without a sign.
questions.hint: Oxygen is usually −2.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the oxidation state of sulfur in SO₃. Give your answer as a number without a sign.
questions.hint: Oxygen is usually −2.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which equation correctly shows phosphorus(V) oxide reacting with water?
questions.hint: The product is a phosphoric acid; check the balance.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which is the correct equation for sodium reacting with water?
questions.hint: Check that both hydrogen and sodium are balanced.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the trend in reactivity with water going down group 1.
questions.hint: Think about how easily the outer electron is lost.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which halogen is the strongest oxidising agent?
questions.hint: Consider which atom best attracts an extra electron.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which mixture would produce a displacement reaction?
questions.hint: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the colour of iodine dissolved in a non-polar solvent such as hexane.
questions.hint: It looks quite different from its aqueous colour.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Explain, with reference to ionisation energy, why potassium reacts more vigorously with water than sodium.
questions.hint: Link atomic size, shielding and how easily the electron is lost.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Explain why period 3 oxides change from ionic to covalent across the period, and describe the effect on the pH of the solutions they form.
questions.hint: Use the electronegativity difference with oxygen.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: The elements in the same period of the periodic table have the same number of:
questions.hint: Think about what row number tells you.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the number of valence electrons in an atom of a group 16 element.
questions.hint: Look at the last digit of the group number.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the block of the periodic table in which sodium is found.
questions.hint: Consider the sub-level of its outermost electron.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: An element has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³. State its period number.
questions.hint: Look at the highest principal quantum number.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which element has the largest atomic radius?
questions.hint: All four are in period 3.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why does atomic radius decrease from left to right across period 3?
options: Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar
Electrons are added to new shells
questions.answer: Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays similar
questions.hint: Compare the pull of the nucleus with the shielding.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of sodium?
questions.hint: Pay attention to the state symbols.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the trend in first ionisation energy down group 1.
questions.hint: Consider how far the outer electron is from the nucleus.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
questions.hint: It is at the top of its group, near the right of its period.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why does electronegativity decrease down group 17?
options: The bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded
Nuclear charge decreases down the group
The atoms have more valence electrons
questions.answer: The bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded
questions.hint: Think about the size of the atom.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Which period 3 oxide is amphoteric?
questions.hint: It reacts with both acids and bases.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What forms when sodium oxide reacts with water?
questions.hint: Metal oxides usually give alkaline solutions.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What forms when sulfur trioxide dissolves in water?
questions.hint: Non-metal oxides often give acidic solutions.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: State the acid–base nature of magnesium oxide.
questions.hint: Think about the type of element bonded to oxygen.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy generally increases across period 3.
questions.hint: Consider nuclear charge, shielding and distance.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Describe the trend in the acid–base character of the oxides across period 3, and explain it in terms of bonding.
questions.hint: Compare the oxides at each end of the period.

comp-hl.topic: A1.4 Translation: compilers, interpreters and virtual machines (HL)

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which type of translator converts a whole source program into machine code before the program runs?
questions.hint: Think about which one produces an executable file in advance.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which translator typically analyses and executes source code one statement at a time?
questions.hint: No separate executable is produced.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Name the first phase of compilation, in which source text is split into tokens.
questions.hint: It works with characters, not with grammar.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What does the parsing stage check?
options: That the token sequence follows the grammar of the language
That the program gives the correct output
That the CPU has enough memory
questions.answer: That the token sequence follows the grammar of the language
questions.hint: Parsing is also called syntax analysis.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which tree structure is normally produced by the parser to represent the program's structure?
questions.hint: Its nodes show how the tokens are grouped by grammar rules.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which order of compiler phases is correct?
questions.hint: Characters must become tokens before structure can be checked.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: How many tokens does a lexical analyser produce from this statement?  total = price * 2 ;
questions.hint: Count each identifier, operator, literal and punctuation mark once.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A statement is missing its closing bracket. In which phase is this error normally detected?
questions.hint: Each individual token may be valid, yet the structure is not.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What is bytecode?
options: An intermediate instruction set designed to be executed by a virtual machine
The binary machine code of one specific CPU
The source code with its comments removed
A list of tokens used only by the parser
questions.answer: An intermediate instruction set designed to be executed by a virtual machine
questions.hint: It sits between high-level source code and native code.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Name the software that executes bytecode on a host computer.
questions.hint: It behaves like an imaginary processor implemented in software.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which is an advantage of distributing a compiled executable rather than source code?
options: Users can run it without having the translator installed
It runs on every type of processor without change
It can be edited directly by users
questions.answer: Users can run it without having the translator installed
questions.hint: Think about what the end user needs on their machine.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Why is an interpreter often convenient during development?
options: It can run code immediately and stop at the first run-time error it reaches
It always produces the fastest possible program
It removes the need for testing
It hides the source code from the programmer
questions.answer: It can run code immediately and stop at the first run-time error it reaches
questions.hint: Consider the edit-and-run cycle.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What does a just-in-time (JIT) compiler do?
options: Translates frequently executed bytecode into native code during execution
Converts machine code back into source code
Checks spelling in comments before compilation
Runs only once when the computer is manufactured
questions.answer: Translates frequently executed bytecode into native code during execution
questions.hint: The clue is when the translation happens.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Compare the use of a compiler and an interpreter for a large commercial application that must run quickly on customers' computers. Refer to execution speed and error reporting.
questions.hint: Consider both the developer's experience and the customer's.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Explain how the combination of bytecode and a virtual machine makes a program portable across different hardware platforms.
questions.hint: What needs to be rewritten for each platform, and what does not?

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Discuss one benefit and one cost of using just-in-time compilation instead of pure interpretation of bytecode.
questions.hint: Think about long-running programs, start-up time and memory.

comp-sl.topic: Programming project: modular program with file input/output

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What is the main benefit of dividing a program into separate modules?
options: Each part can be understood, tested and reused more easily
The program no longer needs any testing
The program always uses less memory
questions.answer: Each part can be understood, tested and reused more easily
questions.hint: Think about working on one part without touching the rest.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What name is given to testing a single module or function on its own?
questions.hint: The smallest testable piece is called a…

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which file mode adds new data to the end of an existing file while keeping its contents?
questions.hint: The word also means 'attach at the end'.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In Python, what happens when an existing text file is opened with mode "w"?
options: New lines are added at the end
questions.hint: Think about what writing from the start means for old data.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Why should a program close a file after writing to it?
options: To make sure buffered data is saved and the resource is released
To delete the file's old name
To convert the file to binary
To make the program compile faster
questions.answer: To make sure buffered data is saved and the resource is released
questions.hint: Output may wait in memory before reaching the disk.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A CSV file has 120 lines, and the first line is a header. How many data records does it contain?
questions.hint: The header does not describe a record.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A file contains the scores 12, 15, 9 and 14, one per line. What average should a correct program output?
questions.hint: Add the values, then divide by how many there are.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A file has three lines containing 4, 5 and 6. The program runs: total = 0, then for each line, total = total + int(line). What is the final value of total?
questions.hint: Trace the loop once for each line.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which data structure is the best choice for looking up student records quickly by a unique ID?
questions.hint: You want to go from a key straight to a value.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A valid mark ranges from 0 to 100 inclusive. Which test value is boundary data?
questions.hint: Look for the value at the edge of the valid range.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: In Python, which exception is raised when a program tries to open a missing file for reading?
questions.hint: The name of the exception describes the problem directly.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Why is passing data through parameters usually better than using global variables?
options: It makes every function run twice
It removes the need for return values
It stops files from being opened
questions.hint: Consider what a function can affect without you noticing.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A program has one function to read a file, one to calculate results and one to display them. Which design idea does this show?
questions.hint: Each function has its own distinct job.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Explain why a function read_scores(filename) that returns a list is better design than one that fills a global list.
questions.hint: Think about reuse, testing and unexpected side effects.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Describe how you would test a module that reads numbers from a file. Include what should happen with a missing file and with an empty file.
questions.hint: Consider normal cases and the cases that could crash the program.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Explain how testing a first version of a small program can lead to improvements in its modular design.
questions.hint: What might testing reveal about how the functions are divided?

econ-hl.topic: Positive externalities and responses to externalities

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: When a positive consumption externality exists, which relationship holds at the free market output?
questions.hint: Third parties also gain from consumption.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Compared with the social optimum, is a good with positive externalities overconsumed or underconsumed in a free market?
questions.hint: Compare the free market quantity with the point where MSB = MSC.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: At the market quantity of a good, MSB is $60 and MPB is $45. What is the external benefit per unit, in dollars?
questions.hint: External benefit is the vertical gap between the two curves.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Market output is 100 units and the socially optimal output is 140 units. The vertical gap between MSB and MSC at market output is $20, and it falls linearly to zero at the optimum. Calculate the welfare loss, in dollars.
questions.hint: The welfare loss is a triangle: ½ × base × height.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Demand is Qd = 200 − 2P and supply is Qs = −40 + 4P. Calculate the free market equilibrium price.
questions.hint: Set Qd equal to Qs.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: For Qd = 200 − 2P and Qs = −40 + 4P, a per-unit producer subsidy of 6 changes supply to Qs = −16 + 4P. Calculate the new quantity traded.
questions.hint: Find the new price first, then substitute it into either function.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which situation best illustrates a positive production externality?
options: A firm trains workers who later bring their skills to other firms
A factory pours waste into a river
A consumer buys a healthier meal for themselves
A firm raises the price of its product
questions.answer: A firm trains workers who later bring their skills to other firms
questions.hint: Look for a benefit to third parties arising from the production process.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: With a positive production externality, how are the cost curves positioned?
questions.hint: Society's cost is reduced by the benefit to third parties.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts a carbon tax with a tradable permit scheme?
options: A tax makes the carbon price more certain; permits make the emissions quantity more certain
A tax fixes total emissions exactly; permits fix the price exactly
Both fix emissions and price exactly
Neither gives firms any incentive to cut emissions
questions.answer: A tax makes the carbon price more certain; permits make the emissions quantity more certain
questions.hint: Ask which variable the government sets directly in each case.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: In economics, what name is given to government rules or legal standards that directly limit polluting activity?
questions.hint: The firm must obey these limits or face a penalty.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which condition identifies the socially optimal level of output?
options: MSB = MPC only when MPC is zero
questions.hint: It compares the full benefits and full costs to society.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: How does an effective awareness campaign about a merit good change the market diagram?
options: MPB shifts to the right, towards MSB
questions.answer: MPB shifts to the right, towards MSB
questions.hint: Better information changes what consumers privately expect to gain.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is a key opportunity cost of subsidising a merit good?
options: Government funds cannot be spent on other priorities
Consumers will pay a much higher price
Producers must stop making the good
questions.answer: Government funds cannot be spent on other priorities
questions.hint: Think about what else the money could have paid for.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Evaluate the view that a carbon tax is a better response to emissions than a system of tradable permits.
questions.hint: Consider certainty, administration, political acceptability and revenue.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Using MSB and MPB, explain why a subsidy on vaccination could increase allocative efficiency. Refer to the welfare loss.
questions.hint: Identify the market failure first, then show how the subsidy changes output.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Discuss whether awareness campaigns are more effective than subsidies for raising the consumption of a merit good.
questions.hint: Consider speed of effect, cost, and consumers with low incomes.

econ-sl.topic: Positive externalities and responses to externalities

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which is an example of a positive consumption externality?
options: A vaccinated person lowers the risk of illness for others
A loud party keeps neighbours awake
A factory smokes up a town
questions.answer: A vaccinated person lowers the risk of illness for others
questions.hint: Look for a benefit that reaches other people.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is the external benefit equal to?
questions.hint: It is the gap between society's benefit and the consumer's own benefit.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is the economic term for a good, such as education, that is under-consumed and benefits society as well as the individual?
questions.hint: The term suggests the good deserves to be consumed more.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: In a market with positive externalities, the free market quantity compared with the social optimum is:
questions.hint: Consumers ignore the benefits to third parties.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The marginal private benefit of a unit is $30 and its external benefit is $8. What is the marginal social benefit, in dollars?
questions.hint: Society's benefit includes both.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A government pays a subsidy of $2 per unit on 5,000 units. How much does this cost the government, in dollars?
questions.hint: Multiply the subsidy by the quantity.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A subsidy paid to producers of a merit good normally shifts which curve, and in which direction?
questions.hint: Think about what happens to producers' costs.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Why does a carbon tax reduce emissions?
options: It raises the cost of burning fossil fuels, encouraging firms to emit less
It bans all fossil fuels immediately
It removes all costs from polluters
questions.answer: It raises the cost of burning fossil fuels, encouraging firms to emit less
questions.hint: The tax puts a price on something that used to be free.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Under a tradable permit scheme, what can a firm do if it cuts emissions cheaply?
options: Sell its unused permits to other firms
questions.answer: Sell its unused permits to other firms
questions.hint: Permits are valuable to firms that find cuts expensive.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: In a tradable permit scheme, what do we call the limit set on total emissions?
questions.hint: The scheme is often described with a phrase ending in 'and trade'.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which is a drawback of regulation as a response to pollution?
options: It gives firms little reason to cut emissions below the required standard
It requires no monitoring at all
It makes every firm's costs fall
questions.answer: It gives firms little reason to cut emissions below the required standard
questions.hint: What happens after a firm meets the limit?

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which is an example of a positive production externality?
options: Research by one firm that other firms can also build on
A firm dumping waste into a lake
A shop offering a loyalty discount
questions.answer: Research by one firm that other firms can also build on
questions.hint: The benefit comes from the production side and reaches third parties.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which policy tries to change behaviour mainly by giving people better information?
questions.hint: Think of advertising about the benefits of healthy habits.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Explain, using MSB and MPB, why education may be under-provided in a free market.
questions.hint: Who gains when one more person is well educated?

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Evaluate the use of subsidies to increase the consumption of a merit good.
questions.hint: Consider both the effect on price and the cost to the government.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Discuss one advantage and one disadvantage of tradable permits compared with direct regulation.
questions.hint: Consider flexibility for firms and the difficulty of setting the cap.

en-hl.topic: The Handmaid's Tale: contexts of production and reception

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In which decade was The Handmaid's Tale first published?
questions.hint: Its context includes the politics of that decade.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the name of the totalitarian regime in the novel?
questions.hint: The name comes from the Bible.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What does 'context of production' refer to?
options: The circumstances in which a text was written
The number of copies a text sold
The present-day reader's personal opinion only
questions.answer: The circumstances in which a text was written
questions.hint: Think of the moment of writing, not of reading.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What does 'context of reception' refer to?
options: How readers in particular times and places understand a text
The grammar used in a text
The physical size of the book
questions.answer: How readers in particular times and places understand a text
questions.hint: It concerns audiences rather than the author.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which 1980s development is most often linked to the novel's context of production?
options: The growing political influence of the religious right in the United States
The invention of the printing press
The end of the Roman Empire
questions.answer: The growing political influence of the religious right in the United States
questions.hint: Consider the anxieties Gilead appears to exaggerate.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What form do the Historical Notes take?
options: A transcript of an academic conference talk
questions.answer: A transcript of an academic conference talk
questions.hint: Consider who is speaking and to what audience.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In what year is the symposium in the Historical Notes set?
questions.hint: It takes place long after Gilead's end.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the surname of the keynote speaker in the Historical Notes?
questions.hint: He is an academic from the University of Cambridge in the novel.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: According to the Historical Notes, how was Offred's account recorded?
options: In a set of radio broadcasts
questions.hint: Her story was spoken, not written down by her.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What important fact about Gilead do readers learn from the Historical Notes?
options: The regime eventually came to an end
The regime took over the whole world
Gilead never existed in any form
questions.answer: The regime eventually came to an end
questions.hint: The speakers look back on it as history.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the main effect of the speaker's jokes in the Historical Notes?
options: They create unease by showing academic detachment from human suffering
They show that the regime was harmless
They prove that Offred invented everything
They make the novel a comedy throughout
questions.answer: They create unease by showing academic detachment from human suffering
questions.hint: Compare his tone with what Offred has endured.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: How does the transcribed form of Offred's account affect the reader's trust in the narrative?
options: It reminds readers that the text has been reconstructed and arranged by others
It proves that every detail is exact
It shows that Offred wrote in perfect order
It has no bearing on reliability
questions.answer: It reminds readers that the text has been reconstructed and arranged by others
questions.hint: Who decided the order of the tapes?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Since the late 2010s, why have red cloaks and white bonnets appeared at public protests?
options: To draw attention to concerns about women's rights
To mark the start of a sports event
questions.answer: To draw attention to concerns about women's rights
questions.hint: This shows the novel's image moving into public debate.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Analyse how the Historical Notes change the reader's understanding of Offred's narrative. Refer to tone and narrative perspective.
questions.hint: Consider what the last section adds and what it leaves unresolved.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Discuss how responses to The Handmaid's Tale may have changed between its first publication and the present day.
questions.hint: Think about time and space, adaptation and current debates.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: To what extent does knowledge of the novel's 1980s context of production deepen a modern reader's interpretation? Justify your view with reference to the text.
questions.hint: Weigh what context explains against what the text can say on its own.

en-sl.topic: The Handmaid's Tale: contexts of production and reception

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Gilead is established on the territory of which country in the novel?
questions.hint: The action takes place around Cambridge, Massachusetts.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Who narrates the main part of the novel?
questions.hint: Her name marks her as belonging to a Commander.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: To which genre does the novel most clearly belong?
questions.hint: It imagines a disturbing future society.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which method did the author say she used when inventing Gilead?
options: Including only practices that had some precedent in human history
Inventing every practice with no basis in reality
Basing it only on a fairy tale
questions.answer: Including only practices that had some precedent in human history
questions.hint: This is why the book's warning feels so plausible.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which 1979 revolution is often cited as relevant to the novel's context, because of the new restrictions placed on women?
questions.hint: Notice the date: the event happened only a few years before the novel.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In relation to the debates of the 1970s and 1980s, what does Offred's mother represent?
questions.hint: Remember what Offred recalls her mother taking part in.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the title of the final section of the novel, set far in the future?
accept: Historical Notes on The Handmaid's Tale
questions.hint: It presents the novel as an object of later study.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: On what kind of recording medium was Offred's story found?
questions.hint: It was an everyday technology of the novel's time of writing.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In the Historical Notes, what were the recordings found inside?
questions.hint: It is a piece of military-style storage.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: How do the academics in the Historical Notes mainly treat Offred's account?
options: As research material to be analysed
As a source of personal guilt
questions.answer: As research material to be analysed
questions.hint: Consider what interests them most about the story.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which question focuses on the novel's context of reception?
options: How have audiences responded since the television adaptation?
What was happening politically when the novel was written?
How many chapters does the novel have?
questions.answer: How have audiences responded since the television adaptation?
questions.hint: Reception concerns audiences after publication.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which question focuses on the novel's context of production?
options: What political anxieties were present when the author wrote?
Why do protesters wear costumes today?
How do schools teach the novel now?
What do online readers post about it?
questions.answer: What political anxieties were present when the author wrote?
questions.hint: Production concerns the time of writing.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Why might a reader today respond differently from a reader in 1985?
options: They read it alongside different current events and debates
The words of the novel change each year
They are not allowed to read the ending
The characters have different names now
questions.answer: They read it alongside different current events and debates
questions.hint: Texts stay fixed, but readers' worlds change.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Explain how the Historical Notes change the way we think about Offred's story.
questions.hint: Consider who controls her words at the end.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Explain one way the novel's 1980s context of production can be seen in the world of Gilead.
questions.hint: Link a detail of the regime to an anxiety of the time.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Why do you think The Handmaid's Tale has received renewed attention in recent years? Support your view with reference to the novel.
questions.hint: Connect a theme in the novel to current public debates.

en_lit-hl.topic: Global issues for the individual oral

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: How many fields of inquiry are there for the individual oral?
questions.hint: Try listing them by subject area.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which of these is one of the fields of inquiry?
questions.hint: Fields of inquiry are broad human concerns, not literary features.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which description best fits a global issue for the individual oral?
options: It is significant, transnational and felt in everyday local contexts
It concerns only one character in one work
It is a technical feature of one poem
It is a fact from an author's life
questions.answer: It is significant, transnational and felt in everyday local contexts
questions.hint: Think about scale as well as everyday experience.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which is the best formulated global issue?
options: How unequal access to education limits personal freedom
A metaphor in the opening chapter
The plot of the first act
questions.answer: How unequal access to education limits personal freedom
questions.hint: A good issue is specific and arguable, not one word or a textual detail.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: A global issue about climate change most clearly belongs to which field of inquiry?
questions.hint: Consider the natural world and human impact on it.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: A global issue about how schools shape moral beliefs most clearly belongs to which field?
questions.hint: Look for the words closest to the issue.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: How many minutes of prepared speaking does the individual oral allow?
questions.hint: The teacher's questions come afterwards.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: How long is the whole individual oral, in minutes, including the teacher's questions?
questions.hint: Add the teacher's questions to the speaking time.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the maximum number of lines in the extract chosen from each work?
questions.hint: The extract should be substantial yet focused.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What percentage of the HL Literature assessment is the individual oral worth?
questions.hint: It carries less weight at HL because of the added HL essay.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What combination of works does the Literature individual oral require?
options: One work originally in the language studied and one studied in translation
Two works by the same author
questions.answer: One work originally in the language studied and one studied in translation
questions.hint: The two works should bring different cultural viewpoints.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the name of the personal collection of reflections and notes kept throughout the course?
questions.hint: It is kept over the two years of the course.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What should a useful portfolio entry for the oral include?
options: Links between passages, authorial choices and an emerging global issue
Only a copy of the plot summary from the internet
A list of the author's awards
questions.answer: Links between passages, authorial choices and an emerging global issue
questions.hint: Think of how it would help you plan your argument.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What should remain central to the oral's analysis?
options: How authorial choices present the global issue in each work
A retelling of each work's plot
The commercial success of each author
questions.answer: How authorial choices present the global issue in each work
questions.hint: Examine the how, not just the what.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Choose two works you have studied. Formulate one global issue they share, name its field of inquiry and justify your choice.
questions.hint: Check that your issue can be seen in both works and in the wider world.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Explain how narrowing a broad topic such as inequality into a precise global issue can improve an individual oral.
questions.hint: Consider focus, choice of extracts and depth of analysis.

en_lit-sl.topic: Global issues for the individual oral

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: How many works must a student use in the individual oral?
questions.hint: One extract comes from each of them.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What percentage of the SL Literature assessment is the individual oral worth?
questions.hint: It has a greater share at SL than at HL.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What term describes a concern with wide impact across borders that is also felt in everyday local life?
questions.hint: This term is the focus of the oral.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which field of inquiry best fits a global issue about belonging in immigrant communities?
questions.hint: Which field concerns who we are and where we belong?

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which field of inquiry best fits a global issue about the abuse of authority by governments?
questions.hint: Which field concerns rulers, rights and fairness?

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which field of inquiry best fits a global issue about how industrial pollution changes rural life?
questions.hint: Think about the effect on land, water and air.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which field of inquiry best fits a global issue about how storytelling helps people imagine change?
questions.hint: Focus on the power of creating.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which of these is NOT suitable as a global issue?
options: The use of a metaphor in one poem
How poverty limits access to healthcare
How gender expectations restrict career choices
questions.answer: The use of a metaphor in one poem
questions.hint: A global issue extends beyond the text itself.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: How long may the extract from each work be?
questions.hint: It must be short enough to discuss in detail.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What follows the student's prepared 10-minute speech?
options: Five minutes of questions from the teacher
A second speech by another student
questions.answer: Five minutes of questions from the teacher
questions.hint: The oral lasts 15 minutes in total.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: A work used in the individual oral cannot also be used in which assessment?
questions.hint: Students need a fresh range of works for the comparative essay.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the main purpose of the learner portfolio?
options: To record personal reflections and develop ideas about the works
To list the prices of books
questions.answer: To record personal reflections and develop ideas about the works
questions.hint: It is a working space for thinking.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which portfolio note is most useful in preparing a global issue?
options: A passage linked to a question about how it shows inequality
A list of the chapter titles only
A note of the book's price
A note of the library's opening hours
questions.answer: A passage linked to a question about how it shows inequality
questions.hint: Useful notes link the text to a wider concern.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Explain why a good global issue must connect to both of the chosen works.
questions.hint: Think about how the oral compares the works' perspectives.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Explain how keeping a learner portfolio across the course could help you prepare your individual oral.
questions.hint: Consider what you would forget without a record.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Why do you think the oral asks students to connect literature with real-world issues? Give a reasoned view.
questions.hint: Think about what literature can show that a news report may not.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript of a spoken announcement: « Je vous rappelle que la réunion de jeudi est reportée à lundi prochain, à quatorze heures. » When will the meeting take place?
questions.hint: Listen for the verb reporter and the 24-hour time.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript: « Malgré la pluie, le festival a attiré plus de visiteurs que l'an dernier. » What happened to attendance?
questions.hint: Malgré introduces an obstacle that did not stop the result.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker says: « Je vais magasiner cette fin de semaine avec ma blonde. » These expressions suggest the speaker is most likely from:
questions.hint: Magasiner and fin de semaine are typical of one North American variety.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A Belgian speaker says the price is « nonante-deux euros ». What is the number?
questions.hint: Nonante replaces quatre-vingt-dix.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A Swiss speaker says there are « septante-cinq participants ». How many participants are there?
questions.hint: Septante replaces soixante-dix.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker from France says « quatre-vingt-dix-sept pour cent ». What is the percentage?
questions.hint: Build the number in parts: 4 × 20 + 17.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript: « Le train n'est pas supprimé : il partira simplement avec vingt minutes de retard. » What is true?
options: The train will leave 20 minutes late
questions.answer: The train will leave 20 minutes late
questions.hint: Pay attention to the negative and to the word retard.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript: « Je n'ai jamais dit qu'il fallait interdire les voitures, seulement les limiter en centre-ville. » What is the speaker's position?
options: Cars should be limited in the city centre
There should be more cars in the centre
Cars should not be regulated at all
questions.answer: Cars should be limited in the city centre
questions.hint: Seulement introduces the actual opinion.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: You hear: « Le nombre de jeunes qui lisent la presse a baissé de moitié en dix ans. » Which is the most efficient note?
questions.hint: Good notes keep key data using symbols.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: In a listening exam, what is the most useful thing to do before the recording begins?
options: Read the questions and predict likely vocabulary
Write out a full essay plan
Close your eyes and ignore the paper
Translate every word on the page into English
questions.answer: Read the questions and predict likely vocabulary
questions.hint: Prepare your ear for what you might hear.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker uses « en revanche » in the middle of an argument. What does it signal?
questions.hint: Listen for a change of direction after it.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: What does the French term « prise de notes » mean in English?
questions.hint: Prendre means to take.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker says: « Il pleut des cordes depuis ce matin. » What does this mean?
questions.hint: Idioms should not be taken literally.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker says: « Ah, bravo, encore une grève ! Quelle excellente nouvelle pour les voyageurs ! » What is the speaker's tone?
questions.hint: Compare the positive words with the situation being described.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: In 3–5 sentences in French, explain which strategies help you understand a speaker with an unfamiliar francophone accent.
questions.hint: Pensez au contexte, aux mots-clés et à la prédiction.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript: « Certains disent que le télétravail isole les gens, mais moi, j'y vois surtout une liberté : moins de transports, plus de temps en famille. » In 3–5 sentences in French, state the speaker's opinion and justify it with details from the transcript.
questions.hint: Identifiez d'abord l'opinion après le mot mais.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript of a spoken announcement: « Le cours de maths commence à neuf heures et quart. » When does the class begin?
questions.hint: Et quart adds a quarter of an hour.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript: « Aujourd'hui, nous allons parler du recyclage dans notre ville. » What is the topic?
questions.hint: The key word looks like its English equivalent.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker says: « Il y a soixante-dix élèves dans le groupe. » How many students are there?
questions.hint: Think 60 + 10.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker says: « Le voyage dure quatre-vingts minutes. » How many minutes does the trip last?
questions.hint: Think 4 × 20.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: In Belgium, what number does « septante » mean?
questions.hint: Sept gives a clue to the first part.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: In Québec, what does « la fin de semaine » usually mean?
questions.hint: Fin means end.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript: « Il ne viendra pas ce soir parce qu'il est malade. » What is true?
options: He is not coming because he is ill
He is coming even though he is ill
He is ill but not sure
questions.answer: He is not coming because he is ill
questions.hint: Listen for ne… pas and the reason after parce que.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: What does the French term « compréhension orale » mean in English?
questions.hint: Orale refers to spoken language.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker says: « Je vais à la bibliothèque après les cours. » In English, name the place the speaker is going to.
questions.hint: A place with many books, though not a bookshop.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: What does listening for gist mean?
questions.hint: You do not need every detail for this.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: You hear: « Léa va à Paris en train mardi. » Which is the best note?
questions.hint: Keep who, where, how and when.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: A speaker says: « D'abord… ensuite… enfin… » What do these words signal?
questions.hint: They help you follow the order.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript: « J'aime ce quartier, mais il est trop bruyant. » What is the speaker's view?
options: The speaker likes the area but finds it too noisy
The speaker hates everything about the area
The speaker finds the area too quiet
The speaker has never been there
questions.answer: The speaker likes the area but finds it too noisy
questions.hint: Mais introduces a drawback.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: In a listening task, what should you do if you miss a word?
options: Keep listening and use the context
Wait for the speaker to spell it
questions.answer: Keep listening and use the context
questions.hint: The next sentence may help.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: In 2–3 sentences in French, say what you do to prepare before a listening exercise.
questions.hint: Pensez aux questions et aux mots-clés.

questions.subject: fre
questions.q: Read this transcript: « Je préfère étudier le matin parce que je suis plus concentré et que la maison est calme. » In 2–3 sentences in French, give the speaker's preference and two reasons.
questions.hint: Cherchez ce qui suit parce que.
